questions.sub_topic: Definition of Lowering of Vapour Pressure
questions.question: When a non-volatile solute is dissolved in a volatile solvent, the lowering of vapour pressure is defined as:
questions.explanation: Lowering of vapour pressure is the absolute difference between the vapour pressure of the pure solvent (\( P^\circ \)) and that of the solution (\( P \)): \( \Delta P = P^\circ - P \).

questions.sub_topic: Concentration Calculations: Molality and Mole Fraction
questions.question: An aqueous solution contains 10% (w/w) glucose (molar mass = 180 g/mol). What is the molality of the solution?
questions.explanation: 10 g glucose in 90 g water. Moles of glucose = 10 / 180 = 0.05556 mol. Mass of water = 0.090 kg. Molality \( m = 0.05556 / 0.090 \approx 0.617\text{ mol/kg} \).

questions.sub_topic: Van't Hoff Factor of Coordination Complexes
questions.question: A 0.01 M aqueous solution of coordination compound \( [\ce{Pt(NH3)4Cl2}]\ce{Cl2} \) freezes at -0.0558°C. Assuming 100% ionization, what is the Van't Hoff factor? (\( K_f \) of water = 1.86 K kg/mol)
questions.explanation: \( [\ce{Pt(NH3)4Cl2}]\ce{Cl2} \to [\ce{Pt(NH3)4Cl2}]^{2+} + 2\ce{Cl^-} \) dissociates into 3 ions per formula unit, giving \( i = 3 \). Theoretical \( \Delta T_f = 3 \times 1.86 \times 0.01 = 0.0558\text{ K} \).

questions.question: Why is it impossible to separate a mixture of 95.6% ethanol and 4.4% water into pure ethanol by standard fractional distillation?
options: A) Water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen at the boiling point of ethanol
B) Ethanol becomes an ionic solid at high temperatures
C) The fractionating column absorbs ethanol completely
D) It forms a minimum boiling azeotrope where the vapour produced has the exact same composition as the boiling liquid
questions.explanation: At 95.6% ethanol, the mixture forms a minimum boiling azeotrope with a constant boiling point (351.15 K). Liquid and vapour have identical compositions, preventing further separation by distillation.

questions.question: When acetic acid is dissolved in water, its molar mass determined cryoscopically is ~35 g/mol, but when dissolved in benzene, it is ~120 g/mol. This is because acetic acid:
options: A) Polymerizes in water into infinite chains
B) Ionizes into ions in polar water (\( i > 1 \)) but associates into dimers in non-polar benzene (\( i < 1 \))
C) Decomposes into methane in benzene
D) Evaporates completely upon dissolving in water
questions.explanation: In water, acetic acid dissociates (\( i \approx 1.7 \)), giving an observed molar mass smaller than 60 g/mol. In non-polar benzene, it forms cyclic hydrogen-bonded dimers (\( i \approx 0.5 \)), giving an observed molar mass of ~120 g/mol.

questions.question: Specific conductivity (\( \kappa \)) of an electrolyte solution is defined as the conductance of:
options: A) 1 mole of electrolyte in 1000 litres of water
B) 1 equivalent of electrolyte between electrodes 1 metre apart
D) A solution of 1 cm length and 1 cm² cross-sectional area (1 cm³ of solution)
questions.explanation: Specific conductivity is the electrical conductance of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area, representing 1 cm³ of the electrolytic solution.

questions.question: During the electrolysis of aqueous \( \ce{NaCl} \), why is chlorine gas (\( E^\circ = +1.36\text{ V} \)) liberated at the anode instead of oxygen gas (\( E^\circ = +1.23\text{ V} \))?
options: A) Chlorine has a lower reduction potential than oxygen
B) The oxidation of water to oxygen requires a large overpotential due to slow reaction kinetics
C) Oxygen is insoluble in water
D) Platinum electrodes absorb chlorine gas
questions.explanation: Although oxidation of water to \( \ce{O2} \) is thermodynamically favored, it involves a kinetically slow 4-electron transfer with a high overpotential, allowing faster evolution of \( \ce{Cl2} \).

questions.question: The electrolyte paste in a commercial Leclanche dry cell consists of a moist mixture of:
questions.explanation: A dry cell uses a moist paste of ammonium chloride (\( \ce{NH4Cl} \)) and zinc chloride (\( \ce{ZnCl2} \)) with carbon and manganese dioxide.

questions.question: Why does rusting of iron take place much more rapidly in saline seawater than in pure freshwater?
options: A) Dissolved \( \ce{NaCl} \) acts as an electrolyte, increasing the electrical conductivity of water and accelerating electrochemical current
B) Seawater contains no dissolved oxygen
C) Sodium ions oxidize iron directly into ferric chloride
D) Chlorine gas forms a protective shield around iron
questions.explanation: Corrosion is an electrochemical process. The presence of dissolved \( \ce{Na^+} \) and \( \ce{Cl^-} \) ions increases electrical conductance of the moisture film, facilitating rapid charge transport between anodic and cathodic micro-regions.

questions.sub_topic: Calculation of Equilibrium Constant from E°
questions.question: For a cell reaction \( \ce{Cu(s) + 2Ag^+(aq) <=> Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2Ag(s)} \), the standard EMF is \( E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.46\text{ V} \). The equilibrium constant \( K_c \) at 298 K is approximately:
questions.explanation: \( E^\circ = \frac{0.059}{n} \log K_c \implies 0.46 = \frac{0.059}{2} \log K_c \implies \log K_c = \frac{0.46 \times 2}{0.059} = \frac{0.92}{0.059} \approx 15.59 \implies K_c = 10^{15.59} \approx 3.9 \times 10^{15} \).

questions.question: Regardless of the reaction order, the rate of a chemical reaction in solution is always expressed in units of:
questions.explanation: Rate of reaction is change in concentration per unit time: \( \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta t} = \frac{\text{mol}/\text{L}}{\text{s}} = \text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} \).

questions.question: In the Arrhenius equation \( k = A e^{-E_a/RT} \), as temperature \( T \to \infty \), the rate constant \( k \) approaches:
questions.explanation: As \( T \to \infty \), \( \frac{E_a}{RT} \to 0 \), so \( e^{-E_a/RT} \to e^0 = 1 \). Therefore, \( k \to A \). The frequency factor represents the maximum theoretical rate constant.

questions.question: Two different reactions have identical activation energies (\( E_a \)) at 300 K. Will their rate constants necessarily be identical?
options: A) Yes, rate constant is determined solely by activation energy
B) Yes, because temperature is the same
C) No, because their frequency factors (A) and collision steric probabilities may be different
D) No, because universal gas constant R varies between reactions
questions.explanation: From \( k = A e^{-E_a/RT} \), even if \( E_a \) and \( T \) are identical, the frequency factor \( A \) (reflecting collision frequency and steric orientation) governs the magnitude of \( k \).

questions.question: The thermal decomposition of dinitrogen pentoxide \( 2\ce{N2O5(g) -> 4NO2(g) + O2(g)} \) follows first-order kinetics. If the reaction is monitored by total gas pressure in a closed vessel, the total pressure:
options: A) Decreases continuously until reaching zero
B) Remains constant throughout the reaction
C) Increases to exactly double the initial pressure
D) Increases continuously and reaches 2.5 times the initial pressure at complete reaction
questions.explanation: 2 moles of gas decompose into \( 4 + 1 = 5 \) moles of gas. Total pressure increases from \( P_0 \) to \( \frac{5}{2} P_0 = 2.5 P_0 \).

questions.question: For a zero-order reaction, the half-life period \( t_{1/2} \) is directly proportional to:
options: A) The square of initial concentration
B) The inverse of initial concentration (\( 1/[A]_0 \))
D) The initial concentration of reactant (\( [A]_0 \))
questions.explanation: For zero order: \( [A] = [A]_0 - kt \). At half-life, \( [A] = [A]_0/2 \implies t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k} \propto [A]_0 \).

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: Cerium exhibits a stable +4 oxidation state (\( \ce{Ce^{4+}} \)) with noble gas configuration \( [\ce{Xe}]\,4f^0 \), making it widely useful in analytical chemistry as:
options: A) A powerful oxidizing agent (reduced to \( \ce{Ce^{3+}} \))
questions.explanation: Although \( \ce{Ce^{4+}} \) has a noble gas configuration, the +3 oxidation state is thermodynamically favored for all lanthanoids; \( \ce{Ce^{4+}} \) has a high \( E^\circ \) (+1.74 V) and acts as a strong oxidizing agent.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: Which of the following pairs of transition metal ions form completely colorless aqueous solutions?
questions.explanation: \( \ce{Sc^{3+}} \) has \( 3d^0 \) (no d-electrons) and \( \ce{Zn^{2+}} \) has \( 3d^{10} \) (completely filled d-orbitals). Neither can undergo d-d electronic transitions, making their solutions colorless.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: Heating solid potassium dichromate with sodium chloride and concentrated sulphuric acid produces reddish-brown vapours of:
questions.explanation: This is the chromyl chloride test for ionic chlorides: \( \ce{K2Cr2O7 + 4NaCl + 6H2SO4 -> 2CrO2Cl2 + 2KHSO4 + 4NaHSO4 + 3H2O} \).

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: The chemistry of actinoids is far more complicated and difficult to study than lanthanoids because actinoids:
options: A) Exhibit a wide range of variable oxidation states and are all radioactive with short half-lives
questions.explanation: 5f, 6d, and 7s electrons are close in energy, leading to numerous oxidation states (+3 to +7). Moreover, all actinoids are radioactive and require specialized radiological handling.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: The irregular variation of standard electrode potentials (\( E^\circ_{\ce{M^{2+}/M}} \)) across the 3d series is primarily due to irregular trends in:
options: A) The sum of the first and second ionization enthalpies and hydration enthalpies
B) The molecular weights of the elements
C) The boiling points of the pure metals
D) The magnetic moments in the solid state
questions.explanation: \( E^\circ \) reflects the enthalpy cycle \( \Delta H = \Delta_{\text{sub}}H + \text{IE}_1 + \text{IE}_2 + \Delta_{\text{hyd}}H \). Irregularities arise from the sum of \( \text{IE}_1 + \text{IE}_2 \) and hydration enthalpies.

questions.question: The coordination number of a central metal atom in a complex is defined as:
options: A) The total number of molecules in the outer sphere
B) The formal oxidation state of the metal atom
C) The number of unpaired electrons in the d-subshell
D) The total number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the metal atom
questions.explanation: Coordination number is the total number of coordinate (dative) bonds formed by ligand donor atoms directly attached to the central metal ion.

questions.question: The coordination complexes \( [\ce{Co(NH3)5(NO2)}]^{2+} \) (yellow-brown) and \( [\ce{Co(NH3)5(ONO)}]^{2+} \) (red) represent:
questions.explanation: The ambidentate ligand \( \ce{NO2^-} \) can coordinate through nitrogen (nitro, \( \ce{-NO2} \)) or through oxygen (nitrito, \( \ce{-ONO} \)), giving linkage isomers.

questions.question: Which of the following changes will INCREASE the crystal field splitting energy (\( \Delta_o \)) of an octahedral coordination complex?
options: A) Increasing the oxidation state of the central metal ion from +2 to +3
B) Replacing a strong field ligand like \( \ce{CN^-} \) with \( \ce{I^-} \)
C) Switching from a 5d transition metal to a 3d transition metal
D) Changing from octahedral geometry to tetrahedral geometry
questions.explanation: Higher positive charge on the metal ion attracts ligands closer, increasing electrostatic repulsion on metal d-orbitals and enlarging \( \Delta_o \).

questions.question: Iron pentacarbonyl (\( [\ce{Fe(CO)5}] \)) has which geometry and hybridization?
questions.explanation: Iron in \( [\ce{Fe(CO)5}] \) has oxidation state zero (\( 3d^6\,4s^2 \)). Strong field CO pairs all 8 valence electrons into four 3d orbitals, leaving one 3d orbital vacant for \( dsp^3 \) trigonal bipyramidal hybridization.

questions.question: Why does anhydrous \( \ce{CuSO4} \) appear white, but hydrated \( \ce{CuSO4.5H2O} \) appears bright blue?
options: A) Anhydrous \( \ce{CuSO4} \) contains no copper atoms
B) Water molecules undergo radioactive fluorescence
C) In anhydrous \( \ce{CuSO4} \), d-orbitals remain degenerate so d-d transitions cannot occur; water ligands split the d-orbitals allowing d-d transitions
D) Hydrated copper loses all its valence electrons
questions.explanation: In absence of ligands, the five 3d orbitals are degenerate and no light absorption occurs. In \( \ce{CuSO4.5H2O} \), water ligands split the d-orbitals; absorption of red-orange light promotes d-d transitions, transmitting complementary blue light.

questions.sub_topic: Boiling Points of Haloalkanes and Branching
questions.question: Among isomeric butyl bromides, which isomer has the lowest boiling point?
questions.explanation: Branching makes the molecule more spherical and compact, reducing surface area and weakening intermolecular van der Waals forces, which lowers the boiling point.

questions.question: Why does the peroxide effect (anti-Markovnikov addition) occur with \( \ce{HBr} \) but NOT with \( \ce{HCl} \) or \( \ce{HI} \)?
options: A) \( \ce{HCl} \) and \( \ce{HI} \) are insoluble in organic solvents
B) Peroxides destroy chlorine and iodine free radicals instantaneously
C) \( \ce{HBr} \) has a symmetrical diatomic structure
D) Both propagation steps in the free radical chain mechanism are exothermic only for \( \ce{HBr} \)
questions.explanation: For \( \ce{HCl} \), the \( \ce{H-Cl} \) bond is too strong for the first propagation step to be exothermic. For \( \ce{HI} \), iodine radicals preferentially recombine into \( \ce{I2} \). Only for \( \ce{HBr} \) are both chain-propagation steps energetically favorable.

questions.question: A pair of enantiomers have identical:
options: A) Melting points, boiling points, and densities, but rotate plane-polarized light in equal and opposite directions
B) Signs of optical rotation and identical reaction rates with chiral enzymes
D) Crystal shapes and different dipole moments
questions.explanation: Enantiomers have identical scalar physical properties (melting point, boiling point, density) in achiral environments, differing only in their interaction with plane-polarized light and chiral reagents.

questions.question: Dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromobutane with alcoholic \( \ce{KOH} \) yields but-2-ene as the major product. Between cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene, the trans isomer predominates because:
options: A) cis-But-2-ene forms intramolecular hydrogen bonds
B) trans-But-2-ene has a higher dipole moment than cis-but-2-ene
C) trans-But-2-ene has less steric repulsion between methyl groups on opposing sides of the double bond
D) cis-But-2-ene is an optically active enantiomer
questions.explanation: In trans-but-2-ene, the bulky methyl groups are on opposite sides of the double bond (180°), minimizing steric hindrance and making it thermodynamically more stable than the cis isomer.

questions.question: When bromobenzene reacts with magnesium turnings in dry diethyl ether, phenylmagnesium bromide is formed. What role does diethyl ether play in this reaction?
options: A) It donates protons to form benzene
B) It acts as a Lewis base, coordinating through oxygen lone pairs to solvate and stabilize the electron-deficient magnesium atom
C) It oxidizes magnesium to magnesium oxide
D) It acts as an inert drying salt
questions.explanation: Ether lone pairs donate electron density to the magnesium center, forming a stable dietherate coordination complex \( \ce{RMgX \cdot 2Et2O} \) that stabilizes the organometallic reagent.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Reaction of Alcohols with Sodium Metal
questions.question: Reaction of ethanol with metallic sodium produces sodium ethoxide with the evolution of:
questions.explanation: \( \ce{2C2H5OH + 2Na -> 2C2H5ONa + H2(g)} \). This reaction demonstrates the acidic character of the alcohol hydroxyl proton.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: In the industrial fermentation of molasses to ethanol, which two enzymes present in yeast catalyze the successive biochemical reactions?
questions.explanation: Invertase hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose and fructose: \( \ce{C12H22O11 + H2O -> C6H12O6 + C6H12O6} \). Zymase then ferments the monosaccharides to ethanol and \( \ce{CO2} \).

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Cresols (methylphenols) are slightly weaker acids than unsubstituted phenol because:
options: A) Methyl group withdraws electrons through mesomeric effect
B) The electron-donating methyl group (+I and hyperconjugation) increases electron density on the ring, destabilizing the phenoxide ion
C) Cresols are insoluble in basic solutions
D) The methyl group forms strong hydrogen bonds with water
questions.explanation: The \( +I \) inductive and hyperconjugative electron donation from the methyl group intensifies the negative charge on the phenoxide oxygen, making cresols slightly weaker acids than phenol.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Attempting to synthesize tert-butyl ethyl ether by heating sodium ethoxide with tert-butyl bromide results almost exclusively in the formation of:
questions.explanation: Sodium ethoxide is a strong nucleophile and strong base. With a tertiary alkyl halide, \( \text{S}_{\text{N}}2 \) attack is sterically blocked, so rapid \( \text{E}2 \) elimination occurs to yield isobutylene.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Treatment of pinacol (2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol) with warm concentrated sulphuric acid yields pinacolone via:
options: A) Oxidative cleavage of the carbon-carbon bond
B) Protonation, loss of water, and a 1,2-methyl shift to the resulting carbocation
questions.explanation: Protonation of one OH group followed by departure of water gives a tertiary carbocation. A 1,2-methyl shift occurs with concomitant lone-pair donation from the remaining OH group, forming pinacolone (\( \ce{(CH3)3C-COCH3} \)).

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Vigorous oxidation of toluene with alkaline \( \ce{KMnO4} \) followed by acidification yields:
questions.explanation: Alkaline \( \ce{KMnO4} \) oxidizes any alkyl side chain having at least one benzylic hydrogen atom completely to potassium benzoate, which upon acidification yields benzoic acid.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Carbonyl compounds react with hydroxylamine (\( \ce{NH2OH} \)) in weakly acidic medium to produce crystalline derivatives called:
questions.explanation: Nucleophilic addition-elimination of hydroxylamine with aldehydes and ketones eliminates water to produce oximes: \( \ce{>C=O + H2N-OH -> >C=N-OH + H2O} \).

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: In the iodoform reaction of acetone with \( \ce{I2} \) and \( \ce{NaOH} \), what carboxylic acid salt is produced alongside iodoform (\( \ce{CHI3} \))?
questions.explanation: \( \ce{CH3COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH -> CHI3(v) + CH3COONa + 3NaI + 3H2O} \). Acetone is cleaved into yellow \( \ce{CHI3} \) and sodium acetate.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Formaldehyde reacts with 50% \( \ce{NaOH} \) via the Cannizzaro reaction. The key hydride-transferring species is:
options: A) The dianion \( [\ce{H-C(O^-)2-H}] \) or monoanion formed by hydroxide addition to formaldehyde
questions.explanation: Hydroxide attacks formaldehyde to form \( \ce{H2C(OH)O^-} \) and under concentrated alkali \( \ce{H2C(O^-)2} \), which transfers its hydride directly to a second molecule of formaldehyde.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Heating malonic acid (propanedioic acid, \( \ce{HOOC-CH2-COOH} \)) at 413-433 K produces:
options: B) Formic acid and carbon monoxide
D) Acetic acid and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Gem-dicarboxylic acids possess two carboxyl groups on the same carbon atom and readily undergo thermal decarboxylation via a 6-membered cyclic transition state to yield acetic acid and \( \ce{CO2} \).

questions.sub_topic: Polarity and Intermolecular Forces in Amines
questions.question: Why do primary and secondary amines have lower boiling points than alcohols of comparable molecular weight?
options: A) Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so N-H...N hydrogen bonds are weaker than O-H...O hydrogen bonds
B) Amines are completely non-polar molecules
C) Amines have higher vapour densities than alcohols
D) Alcohols contain no hydrogen atoms
questions.explanation: Electronegativity of oxygen (3.5) is higher than nitrogen (3.0), making O-H bonds more polar and intermolecular hydrogen bonds significantly stronger in alcohols than in amines.

questions.question: Reduction of ethanenitrile (\( \ce{CH3CN} \)) with sodium and boiling ethanol yields:
questions.explanation: Reduction of alkyl cyanides with sodium and ethanol (or \( \ce{LiAlH4} \)) adds 4 hydrogen atoms across the triple bond to yield primary amines (Mendius reaction): \( \ce{CH3CN + 4[H] -> CH3CH2NH2} \).

questions.question: Why is the sulfonamide formed by reacting ethylamine with benzenesulphonyl chloride soluble in aqueous \( \ce{KOH} \)?
options: A) The hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen is strongly acidic due to the electron-withdrawing sulphonyl group
B) The sulfonamide undergoes instant hydrolysis to potassium sulphate
C) Ethylamine dissolves potassium hydroxide crystals
D) The benzene ring becomes non-polar in alkaline solution
questions.explanation: In \( \ce{C6H5SO2-NH-C2H5} \), the strong \( -M/-I \) effect of \( -\ce{SO2}- \) makes the remaining N-H proton acidic. Base abstracts this proton, forming a water-soluble potassium salt.

questions.question: When benzenediazonium chloride is added to an alkaline solution of \( \beta \)-naphthol (2-naphthol), coupling occurs exclusively at which position of naphthalene?
options: D) C1 position (alpha position adjacent to -OH group)
questions.explanation: In 2-naphthol, position 1 is uniquely activated for electrophilic aromatic substitution without disrupting the aromaticity of both fused rings in the transition state, forming 1-(phenyldiazenyl)naphthalen-2-ol (Sudan I red dye).

questions.question: In the modern modification of Gabriel phthalimide synthesis (Ing-Manske procedure), the N-alkylphthalimide is cleaved to yield the primary amine by treatment with:
options: A) Concentrated hydrochloric acid at 500 K
questions.explanation: Hydrazinolysis with hydrazine hydrate cleaves N-alkylphthalimides under very mild conditions, precipitating insoluble phthalhydrazide and releasing pure primary amine with excellent yields.

questions.question: Cellulose, the chief structural component of plant cell walls, is a linear unbranched polymer composed of:
options: B) \( \beta \)-D-glucose units joined by \( \beta \)(1->4) glycosidic linkages
D) D-galactose units joined by peptide bonds
questions.explanation: Cellulose consists of repeating \( \beta \)-D-glucopyranose units linked by \( \beta \)-1,4-glycosidic bonds, forming rigid linear chains stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonding.

questions.question: Amino acids exhibit amphoteric behavior in aqueous solution because they:
options: A) Dissociate into metallic cations and halide anions
B) Contain both a basic \( -\ce{NH2} \) (or \( -\ce{NH3^+} \)) group and an acidic \( -\ce{COOH} \) (or \( -\ce{COO^-} \)) group
C) Are completely insoluble in neutral water
D) Contain only non-polar hydrocarbon chains
questions.explanation: In zwitterionic form, the \( -\ce{COO^-} \) group can accept a proton from acids, while the \( -\ce{NH3^+} \) group can donate a proton to bases, exhibiting amphoteric reactivity.

questions.question: The remarkable substrate specificity of enzymes is explained by the Lock and Key hypothesis proposed by Emil Fischer, which postulates that:
options: A) Enzymes permanently alter the substrate by dissolving its peptide backbone
B) The enzyme active site possesses a predefined rigid geometric shape complementary to the substrate
C) Any organic molecule can fit into any enzyme active site
D) Substrate molecules change their elemental composition upon contact
questions.explanation: The Lock and Key model postulates that the enzyme's active site (lock) has a fixed, rigid 3D conformation into which only a specific substrate (key) fits with structural complementarity.

questions.question: Rickets in children, characterized by soft and deformed bones, is caused by the dietary deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin D regulates calcium and phosphate absorption in the intestine; its deficiency leads to defective bone mineralization, causing rickets in children.

questions.question: The primary sequence of the hormone insulin was first elucidated by Frederick Sanger. Structurally, human insulin consists of:
options: A) Chain A (21 amino acids) and Chain B (30 amino acids) linked by two interchain disulfide bridges
B) A single continuous chain of 100 amino acids without sulfur
C) Chain A (50 amino acids) and Chain B (50 amino acids) linked by peptide bonds
D) Four identical beta-pleated sheets without covalent linkages
questions.explanation: Insulin consists of 51 amino acids distributed across two chains: chain A (21 residues) and chain B (30 residues), connected by two interchain disulfide bonds (plus one intrachain bridge in A).
